# Summary of John L. Pollock
John L. Pollock (1940–2009) was an American philosopher known for foundational work in epistemology and artificial intelligence. He completed triple majors in physics, mathematics, and philosophy, earning his Ph.D. from UC Berkeley. Pollock held faculty positions at multiple universities, spending most of his career at the University of Arizona, where he helped establish the Cognitive Science Program.
Pollock's major philosophical contributions include his influential book *Knowledge and Justification* , which introduced the concept of defeasible reasoning to mainstream epistemology. He developed key concepts such as "undercutting defeat" and "rebutting defeat" that became central to the study of non-monotonic reasoning in philosophy and AI. Throughout his career, Pollock advanced the theory and implementation of artificial reasoning systems, notably through his OSCAR project, a LISP-based AI that operationalized his theories of interest-based and defeasible reasoning. He also made significant contributions to the philosophy of probability and induction through his work on nomic probability, and published numerous influential books and papers spanning logic, epistemology, artificial intelligence, and semantics.
